newsitem.title: SPAIN: U.S. seeks strong signal on Baltics from NATO.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks strong signal on Baltics from NATO.

text.p: The United States wants a NATO summit this week to send a "very strong signal" that the Baltic states are welcome to seek NATO membership in future, despite strong Russian opposition, U.S. officials said on Sunday.

A senior official briefing reporters aboard the plane bringing Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to Madrid for the 16-nation summit said the question of the Baltics was "clearly one of the very tough issues" facing the alliance.

None of the Baltic states -- Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia -- will be in the first wave of ex-communist countries which Tuesday's summit will invite to apply to join NATO, but their possible future membership is already looming as an issue.

Russia, which has grudgingly accepted NATO expansion to include some East European states, has threatened to review its ties with the alliance if the Baltic states, which were under Soviet rule from World War Two to 1991, are admitted.
But the U.S. official, speaking on condition he was not identified, said the summit must stress that no one was excluded.

"We would hope that both in the communique and also in what is said by individual leaders in Madrid there would be a very strong signal that the Baltic states are eligible and that they will be encouraged to pursue their aspirations for NATO membership," he said.
Albright will meet Baltic leaders during a post-summit visit next weekend to the Lithuanian capital Vilnius.

The United States wants the summit to invite Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to apply to join. But up to nine other NATO countries, led by France, believe Romania and Slovenia should also be invited.
"The differences that you all know... are still there," the U.S. official said. "We continue to feel very strongly that for now, three is the right number."
He said Washington was keen that there should be "a good, productive airing" at Tuesday's summit of the issues facing NATO, including the points on which the allies disagreed.
U.S. officials say that although they expect differing opinions to be voiced, they are confident that in the end the view of the United States, the acknowledged alliance leader, will prevail.
